title: A quantitative bias analysis verdict scored as a classifier
question: How often does a QBA declare a MAIC decision robust when the true bias would reverse it, how does that depend on the elicited region rather than the method, and does oracle recovery reveal it?
design: Unanchored MAIC with an unmeasured binary confounder; elicited bias regions with exclusion probability set directly, three error directions and three widths; grid and probabilistic QBA scored on false reassurance and false fragility; 18 cells, 2000 replicates each.
answer: A QBA's robust verdict is only as good as the elicited region. When the region contains the true bias the grid never reassures falsely (an exact property); with elicitation errors scaled to the region it reassured falsely at most 17% of the time the true bias reversed the decision, but with the common region centered at zero bias it did so 78%, 37% and 9% of the time at half-widths 0.05, 0.15 and 0.3. Probabilistic QBA avoided false reassurance by calling 62% to 85% of sound decisions fragile. Oracle recovery was nominal throughout and revealed none of this.
findings: Exact checks: zero grid false reassurance in every replicate whose region contained the true bias and at exclusion probability 0.

Primary (exclusion 0.1, half-width 0.15): grid false reassurance 0.008 (symmetric) and 0.020 (understated); false fragility 0.333 and 0.279. Probabilistic QBA 0.000 and 0.710 to 0.748. Neither dominated.
Refuting sentence fails: oracle coverage 0.951 to 0.961 in every scenario while grid false reassurance under a zero-centered region was 0.776, 0.370 and 0.092.
The probabilistic QBA's own Monte Carlo error (1000 draws) changed its verdict in 0.9% to 1.6% of analyses.
not_answered: One scalar bias parameter; effect modification and overlap not varied; the elicitation model is assumed. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Robustness classification: whether the decision at the true bias equals the unadjusted decision
methods_compared: deterministic grid (equivalent to bounds and tipping point for one scalar bias)
n_sim: 2000 per scenario, 36,000 in total, each scored under 21 elicitation settings
